verdicts.trueWording: the prose is (deliberately) dry and staid
verdicts.note: Irish Times raw page fetched 200. Sentence reads: "Because the book is masquerading as an historical document the prose is (deliberately) dry and staid". Quote 'dry and staid' word for word; both limbs (masquerade-as-history cause, deliberate dryness) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: characters can live full lives in a single paragraph
verdicts.note: Same sentence continues: "the events relayed are so dense that characters can live full lives in the space of a single paragraph". Quote verbatim; density limb and paragraph limb both present.

verdicts.trueWording: It's hard to root for anyone as they rarely stick around
verdicts.note: Quote 'an extremely unreliable narrator' is verbatim ("purportedly written by Archmaester Gyldayn, an extremely unreliable narrator"), and the not-investing limb is on the page ("It's hard to root for anyone as they rarely stick around long enough for us to get to know them"). But the review attributes that difficulty to the events' density, not to narratorial distance; the two facts sit in adjacent sentences with no causal link drawn.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the causal limb 'that distance keeps readers from investing' - Nugent attributes the failure to root to characters not sticking around, never to the unreliable narrator's distance

verdicts.trueWording: if you enjoyed The Silmarillion, you'll like this; if not, steer clear
verdicts.note: Page: "a helpful yardstick exists: if you enjoyed JRR Tolkien's The Silmarillion, you'll like this. If not, steer clear." Quote 'If not, steer clear.' verbatim; 'rule of thumb' matches 'yardstick'; byline is Patrick Nugent, dated Sat Feb 16 2019.

verdicts.trueWording: at least three chapters so packed with Machiavellian machinations
verdicts.note: Page: "There are at least three chapters in here that are so packed with Machiavellian machinations, political intrigue and set-pieces that any one of them alone could be the basis for the next Westeros-based TV series." Quote verbatim; 'sustain a series of its own' = 'be the basis for the next Westeros-based TV series'.

verdicts.trueWording: not everyone is down on the book; angriest of all is GQ
verdicts.note: winteriscoming.net raw page fetched 200. Every named limb checks out: Independent ("the prose is so dry that even ... a battle in the sky ... manages to fall as flat"); GQ Levesley ("a dry, dusty historical screed"); Rifkind of The Times ("one long synopsis for about 50 books", introduced as "beyond not liking the style"); Dan Jones ("strictly chronological telling ... evokes the same propulsive storytelling"); Chris Lough of Tor.com ("the best Song of Ice and Fire book in 18 years"). The roundup's own pivot is "But not everyone is down on the book", so the sharp division is the page's framing. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM only because the claim supplies no quotation to match.

verdicts.trueWording: links Independent, PW, GQ, The Times, Sunday Times, Tor.com, Mental Floss
verdicts.note: The link set is exactly right, confirmed by parsing every href in the raw HTML: independent.co.uk (O'Connor), publishersweekly.com/978-1-5247-9628-0, gq-magazine.co.uk/article/fire-and-blood-review, thetimes.co.uk (Rifkind), thetimes.co.uk/magazine (Dan Jones, Sunday Times), tor.com/2018/11/21, mentalfloss.com - and no nytimes.com, theguardian.com or vox.com link anywhere on the page. The final limb is the problem: a roundup page cannot attest that no such reviews exist or that a search failed to find them. WebSearch could not settle it either (those three domains are blocked to the agent), so the limb stays unverified rather than contradicted.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'and none were found' - an assertion about the researcher's own search, which the roundup page cannot support either way

verdicts.trueWording: the prose is so dry that a battle in the sky falls flat
verdicts.note: Independent raw page fetched 200 (redirects to the-independent.com). Page: "Martin appears to have made the assumption that historical writing should be dry and clinical, and that the excitement of the events themselves should be left to do the talking. Yet the prose is so dry that even descriptions of a battle in the sky between two brothers manages to fall as flat as the losing Targaryen and his dragon." Quote verbatim; all three limbs present. The page hedges with "appears to have made the assumption" where the claim says "assumes" - a hedge stripped, not a limb added.

verdicts.trueWording: sheer scale and exhaustive detail feels like assigned homework
verdicts.note: Page: "the sheer scale and exhaustive detail in Fire and Blood makes reading it feel more like you've been assigned a mildly interesting, but often tedious, piece of homework." Quote verbatim. Both adjectives hold of the book on this page - dense ('sheer scale and exhaustive detail') and name-heavy ('several characters have incredibly similar names (at least six are called Aegon)') - though the homework sentence itself is pinned to scale and detail, not to the names.

verdicts.trueWording: not in its length but in its complexity; first 100 pages OK
verdicts.note: Page: "the main problem with Fire and Blood lies not in its length (an eye-watering 706 pages) but in its complexity. The first 100 pages are OK, but as the history continues, the reader struggles to keep up. It doesn't help that several characters have incredibly similar names (at least six are called Aegon)". Quote verbatim; complexity-over-length limb and hundred-pages limb both confirmed by string match.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin's publisher describes the scope and grandeur of Gibbon's
verdicts.note: Page: "Fire and Blood is written as an in-universe account (purportedly) by the Archmaester Gyldayn of the Citadel, in a style that Martin's publisher describes as possessing the 'scope and grandeur of Gibbon's The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire'." Quote verbatim, attribution to the publisher explicit, in-universe limb explicit. (GQ independently corroborates, calling it the dust jacket.)

verdicts.trueWording: really, really committed to a dry, dusty historical screed
verdicts.note: GQ raw page fetched 200. Page: "Martin is really, really committed to a dry, dusty historical screed for his style of writing." Quote verbatim; 'wholly committed' renders 'really, really committed' and 'the book's style' renders 'his style of writing'.

verdicts.trueWording: fascinating situations over in sentences; men get pages of bluster
verdicts.note: Page: "elder sister Velenya engages in diplomatic parleys with powerful Westerosi women and these fascinating situations are over in sentences - whereas indistinguishable men get pages of bluster. The fault of the maester's voice the piece is written in? A statement on how history brushes over women's impact? Almost certainly, considering Martin loves creating fully fleshed out women characters." Quote verbatim; every limb present. Levesley poses the maester's-voice and the statement-on-history readings as rhetorical questions and then answers them "Almost certainly", so the endorsement the claim reports is the page's own.

verdicts.trueWording: just like Homer, a pageant of almost indistinguishable names
verdicts.note: Page: "Just like Homer, Martin relishes a pageant of almost indistinguishable names to show the scope of combat. But, unlike Homer, he's not a big fan of generating much narrative tension". Quote verbatim; the like-Homer limb and the unlike-Homer tension limb are consecutive sentences.

verdicts.trueWording: only last a few pages before a return to brisk summary
verdicts.note: Publishers Weekly raw page fetched 200, review dated 11/19/2018. Page: "there are entertaining snatches of dialogue and detailed depictions of battles, but they only last a few pages before a return to brisk summary." Quote verbatim; dialogue limb, battles limb and few-pages limb all present.
